en.correct: the presence of pathogenic bacteria and their toxins in the bloodstream, often causing a severe systemic illness
distractors: a localized bacterial infection confined to a single organ
the presence of antibodies circulating in the blood after recovery

example.text: Untreated septicemia can rapidly progress to organ failure and shock.

en.correct: testing negative for the presence of a specific antibody in the blood
distractors: testing positive for the presence of a specific antibody in the blood
having no detectable white blood cells in a blood sample

example.text: Despite clear symptoms, the patient remained seronegative during the early window period of infection.

en.correct: testing positive for the presence of a specific antibody in the blood
distractors: testing negative for the presence of a specific antibody in the blood
showing no clinical signs of infection despite laboratory abnormalities

example.text: Being seropositive for the virus indicated the patient had been exposed at some point in the past.

en.correct: describing an infection or disease that produces no noticeable symptoms
distractors: describing a disease so severe it requires immediate hospitalization
describing an infection confirmed only through post-mortem examination

example.text: Many carriers experience a subclinical infection, spreading the pathogen without ever feeling ill.

en.correct: a new infection that occurs on top of a previous one, often involving a different or resistant organism
distractors: the first infection a host experiences with a particular pathogen
an infection that resolves without any treatment

example.text: Prolonged antibiotic use left the patient vulnerable to a fungal superinfection.

en.correct: relating to or forming a mass of fused, multinucleated cells
distractors: relating to cells that remain strictly separate and individual
relating to the destruction of infected cells by the immune system

example.text: Respiratory syncytial virus causes infected airway cells to fuse together into large multinucleated masses.

en.correct: the transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another by a bacteriophage
distractors: the direct uptake of free DNA from the environment by a bacterium
the transfer of genetic material through direct cell-to-cell contact

example.text: Transduction by a phage allowed the resistance gene to spread to a previously susceptible bacterial strain.

en.correct: a virus historically used in the smallpox vaccine, related to but distinct from the smallpox-causing variola virus
distractors: the causative agent of smallpox itself
a bacterial toxin used in early vaccine preparations

example.text: Vaccinia virus was used for decades to induce protective immunity against smallpox.

en.correct: a complete, infectious virus particle existing outside a host cell
distractors: the genetic material of a virus once it has entered a host cell
an antibody specifically produced to target viral particles

example.text: Each infected cell released thousands of new virions into the surrounding tissue.

en.correct: relating to a chemical compound foreign to a living organism, such as a drug or pollutant
distractors: relating to a compound naturally synthesized by the organism itself
relating to genetic material transferred between two different species

example.text: The liver metabolizes many xenobiotic compounds before they can accumulate to toxic levels.

en.correct: a substance added to a vaccine to enhance the immune response it provokes
distractors: the antigenic component of a vaccine that the immune system recognizes
a preservative added solely to extend a vaccine's shelf life

example.text: Aluminum salts are commonly used as an adjuvant to boost the vaccine's effectiveness.

en.correct: the clumping together of particles, such as bacteria or red blood cells, typically caused by antibody cross-linking
distractors: the complete dissolution of cells following antibody binding
the migration of clumped cells toward a chemical signal

example.text: Agglutination of the bacteria in the test tube confirmed the presence of specific antibodies in the serum.

en.correct: relating to an accelerated, heightened immune response upon second exposure to an antigen, due to immunological memory
distractors: relating to the very first immune response to a novel antigen
relating to a weakened response caused by immune exhaustion

example.text: The anamnestic response produced antibodies far faster and in greater quantity than the initial exposure had.

en.correct: the practice of using chemical agents to prevent or reduce microbial contamination on living tissue
distractors: the complete destruction of all microorganisms on an inanimate surface
the process by which the body clears an established infection

example.text: Antisepsis of the surgical site with an antimicrobial solution reduced the risk of postoperative infection.

en.correct: an antibody that specifically neutralizes a bacterial or other biological toxin
distractors: a chemical compound used to destroy toxin-producing bacteria
a vaccine formulation containing an attenuated toxin-producing organism

example.text: Antitoxin was administered promptly to neutralize the circulating diphtheria toxin.

en.correct: the presence of viable bacteria circulating in the bloodstream
distractors: the presence of bacterial toxins alone in the bloodstream without live organisms
a localized bacterial infection confined to the skin

example.text: Blood cultures confirmed bacteremia, prompting immediate intravenous antibiotic therapy.

en.correct: a firm, typically painless ulcer that forms at the initial site of certain infections, notably syphilis
distractors: a fluid-filled blister characteristic of viral skin infections
a raised, itchy rash caused by an allergic reaction

example.text: The painless chancre on the skin was the first visible sign of the primary infection.

en.correct: a process by which bacteria transfer genetic material directly between cells through physical contact, often via a pilus
distractors: the uptake of free DNA fragments from the surrounding environment
the transfer of genetic material by means of a bacteriophage

example.text: Through conjugation, the resistant bacterium passed its plasmid directly to a neighboring susceptible cell.

en.correct: an imbalance in the composition of the normal microbial community, often associated with disease
distractors: the complete absence of microorganisms within a host system
the process by which beneficial bacteria colonize a newborn's gut

example.text: Antibiotic overuse can trigger gut dysbiosis, allowing opportunistic pathogens to flourish.

en.correct: a highly resistant, dormant structure formed by certain bacteria to survive extreme environmental conditions
distractors: a membrane-bound organelle found in eukaryotic cells
a toxin released when a bacterial cell is destroyed

example.text: The bacterium's endospore can withstand boiling, radiation, and years of desiccation before germinating.

en.correct: a toxin that specifically targets the cells lining the intestine, often causing diarrhea
distractors: a toxin that primarily damages the respiratory epithelium
an antibody produced against toxins found in the gut

example.text: The enterotoxin produced by the bacterium caused the intestinal cells to secrete excess fluid, resulting in diarrhea.

en.correct: relating to organisms whose cells contain a membrane-bound nucleus and other complex organelles
distractors: relating to organisms whose genetic material floats freely in the cytoplasm
relating to viruses that lack any cellular structure

example.text: Antifungal drugs must target processes unique to eukaryotic cells without harming the human host.

en.correct: a widespread skin rash that often accompanies a systemic infection, especially in children
distractors: a localized skin infection confined to a single lesion
a chronic autoimmune skin condition unrelated to infection

example.text: The characteristic exanthem appeared across the child's trunk a few days after the fever began.

en.correct: relating to an experimental animal raised in a controlled environment with a known and defined microbial population, including germ-free
distractors: relating to an animal exposed to an uncontrolled, natural microbial environment
relating to an organism genetically engineered to lack an immune system

example.text: Gnotobiotic mice, colonized with a single defined bacterial species, let researchers isolate that microbe's effects.

en.correct: a condition in which the immune system's capacity to fight infection is reduced or absent
distractors: a condition in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues
an excessive immune response to a normally harmless antigen

example.text: Children born with severe combined immunodeficiency are highly vulnerable to infections from birth.

en.correct: capable of altering or regulating the activity of the immune system
distractors: incapable of producing any effect on immune cell activity
relating exclusively to the destruction of cancer cells

example.text: The drug's immunomodulatory effects helped dampen the excessive inflammatory response.

en.correct: a state in which a pathogen, especially a virus, persists within the host in an inactive form without producing symptoms
distractors: the incubation period between exposure and the onset of symptoms
the phase of active viral replication and particle release

example.text: Herpesviruses can establish latency in nerve cells, reactivating unpredictably years later.

en.correct: having a particular affinity for infecting lymphoid cells or tissue
distractors: having a particular affinity for infecting skin cells
incapable of infecting any cells of the immune system

example.text: The lymphotropic virus preferentially infected and depleted a specific subset of T cells.

en.correct: describing an organism that grows best at moderate temperatures, typically those found in the human body
distractors: describing an organism that thrives only at extremely high temperatures
describing an organism that requires an oxygen-free environment to grow

example.text: Most human pathogens are mesophilic, growing optimally near normal body temperature.

en.correct: the collective community of microorganisms living in or on a particular environment, such as the human gut
distractors: a single dominant species of bacteria isolated from a host
the set of antibodies produced against a host's normal flora

example.text: Disruption of the gut microbiota by antibiotics can have lasting effects on digestion and immunity.

en.correct: a chemical agent used in staining procedures to fix or intensify a dye's binding to a microbial specimen
distractors: a nutrient-rich substance added to promote bacterial growth in culture
an antibody used to visually label a specific antigen

example.text: In the Gram stain procedure, iodine acts as a mordant that helps trap the crystal violet dye within the cell wall.

en.correct: an agent, such as certain chemicals or radiation, that increases the rate of genetic mutation in an organism
distractors: an agent that repairs existing mutations within a genome
an enzyme that specifically degrades foreign genetic material

example.text: Ultraviolet light acts as a mutagen, damaging bacterial DNA and occasionally inducing resistance mutations.

en.correct: causing the death of tissue
distractors: promoting the regeneration of damaged tissue
confined strictly to superficial skin layers without deeper damage

example.text: The necrotizing infection destroyed soft tissue so rapidly that emergency surgery was required.

en.correct: an infectious agent composed solely of misfolded protein, capable of inducing normal proteins to misfold as well
distractors: a virus that lacks any protein coat surrounding its genome
a bacterial toxin that disrupts neuronal signaling

example.text: Prions cause degenerative brain diseases without containing any genetic material of their own.

en.correct: the dormant form of a bacteriophage genome integrated within a bacterial chromosome
distractors: a fully assembled virus particle ready to infect a new cell
a bacterial gene that confers resistance to phage infection

example.text: Certain toxin genes are carried by a prophage integrated into the bacterium's own chromosome.

en.correct: producing or causing the formation of pus
distractors: preventing the immune system from forming pus at a wound site
relating exclusively to viral rather than bacterial infections

example.text: Staphylococcus aureus is a classic pyogenic organism, frequently causing abscesses filled with pus.

en.correct: produced by combining genetic material from different sources, typically through laboratory techniques
distractors: derived exclusively from a single natural, unmodified organism
incapable of being expressed in a host cell system

example.text: The recombinant vaccine antigen was produced by inserting the viral gene into a yeast expression system.
